title: Color temperature
description: Property of light sources related to black-body radiation
wiki_lead:
Color temperature is a parameter describing the color of a visible light source by comparing it to the color of light emitted by an idealized opaque, non-reflective body, known as a black body. The temperature of the ideal emitter that matches the color most closely is defined as the color temperature of the original visible light source. The color temperature scale describes only the color of light emitted by a light source, which may actually be at a different (and often much lower) temperature.
Color temperature has applications in lighting, photography, videography, publishing, manufacturing, and other fields. In practice, color temperature is most meaningful for light sources that correspond somewhat closely to the color of some black body, i.e., light in a range going from red to orange to yellow to white to bluish white. Although the concept of correlated color temperature extends the definition to any visible light, the color temperature of a green or a purple light rarely is useful information. Color temperature is conventionally expressed in kelvins, using the symbol K, which are units for absolute temperature.

Color temperature is conventionally expressed in kelvins, using the symbol K, which are units for absolute temperature.


Categorizing different lighting

The color temperature of the electromagnetic radiation emitted from an ideal black body is the black body's surface temperature in kelvins, or alternatively in micro reciprocal degrees (mired). This permits the definition of a standard by which light sources are compared.
If a hot surface is not an ideal black-body radiator, the color temperature of the light it emits is not the actual temperature of the surface. An incandescent lamp's light is thermal radiation, and the bulb approximates an ideal black-body radiator, so its color temperature is essentially the temperature of the filament. Thus a relatively low temperature emits a dull red and a high temperature emits the almost white of the traditional incandescent light bulb. Metal workers are able to judge the temperature of hot metals by their color, from dark red to orange-white and then white (see red heat).
Many other light sources, such as fluorescent lamps, or light emitting diodes (LEDs) emit light primarily by processes other than thermal radiation. This means that the emitted radiation does not follow the form of a black-body spectrum. These sources are assigned what is known as a correlated color temperature (CCT). CCT is the color temperature of a black-body radiator which to human color perception most closely matches the light from the lamp. Because such an approximation is not required for incandescent light, the CCT for an incandescent light is simply its unadjusted temperature, derived from comparison to a black-body radiator.


The Sun
The Sun closely approximates a black-body radiator. The effective temperature, defined by the total radiative power per square unit, is 5,772 K. The color temperature of sunlight above the atmosphere is about 5,900 K.

grok_lead: Color temperature is a metric used to describe the color appearance of a visible light source by comparing it to the chromaticity of light emitted by an idealized blackbody radiator at a specific absolute temperature, expressed in kelvins (K). It quantifies the perceived warmth or coolness of the light, with lower values (e.g., around 2,000â3,000 K) appearing reddish or yellowish and higher values (e.g., 5,000â10,000 K) appearing bluish or whitish, based on the Planckian locus in the chromaticity diagram. This concept originates from blackbody radiation physics, where the spectral distribution of emitted light shifts from red to blue as temperature increases. In practical applications, color temperature, often specified as correlated color temperature (CCT) for non-blackbody sources, plays a crucial role in lighting design, photography, and display technology to ensure accurate color rendering and visual comfort. For instance, incandescent bulbs typically have a CCT of 2,700 K, mimicking warm candlelight, while daylight approximates 5,500â6,500 K, influencing white balance settings in cameras to compensate for ambient illumination. Standards from organizations like the Illuminating Engineering Society (IES) and the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) define CCT calculation methods, ensuring consistency across industries such as LED manufacturing and architectural lighting. Related metrics, like Duv, further refine this by measuring deviation from the ideal blackbody curve, affecting perceived tint (e.g., greenish or pinkish). The scale extends beyond visible light sources to encompass phenomena like stellar classification, where stars are categorized by effective temperatures correlating to their colors, from cool red giants at about 3,000 K to hot blue stars exceeding 25,000 K. In modern contexts, tunable LED systems allow dynamic adjustment of color temperature to match circadian rhythms or enhance mood in environments like offices and homes.
